OWNER GOAL: 'all mods autoupdate with compatible versions' for the one-click mod installs. Existing pieces on main: the one-click installers (K1: lib/mods*, worker/game-mods.ts, worker/mods-guest-ssh.ts, tests test/mods-installers.test.ts), the NX Labs catalog with versions/loaders/game-version compat (K2: lib/modsync/*, GameMod/ModVersion tables, resolveLocal()), the server-software jar mirror + pinning for Minecraft (lib/mcjars/*, McJarPin, worker/mcmirror.ts), game auto-update (worker/game-update.ts + lib/game-update-verify.ts + components/customer/GameAutoUpdate.tsx), the D1 SweepRunner (worker/sweeps.ts: register sweeps via add(...) in registerSweeps in worker/index.ts), and the Valheim KB section at the end of docs/DOCUMENTATION.md (esp. the 'client parity' trap: gameplay mods must be the SAME version on every player's client or Valheim refuses the connection — customer Jay's friends could not join for exactly that reason).
BUILD: (1) Installed-mod records per server (additive schema, reuse K1's if it already has one — read it first): what/which version/which provider/which file, pinned flag, autoUpdate mode per mod and per server (OFF | NOTIFY | AUTO), clientRequired flag (from provider metadata: Modrinth client_side/server_side, Thunderstore/others heuristics + a curated override list for Valheim where almost every gameplay mod needs client parity), last check, last update, failure history. (2) Compatibility resolver (pure, unit-tested, no I/O): given the server's game + game version + loader/modloader (Minecraft: type + version from McJarPin/gameVariant; Valheim: BepInEx + current game build; others: per lib/games.ts), pick the newest COMPATIBLE version of each installed mod and resolve its required dependencies transitively (conflict/incompatible detection, version ranges, loader mismatch, 'no compatible version' as an explicit state, never downgrade unless asked), explain every decision in a human-readable reason string. (3) Auto-update engine: a worker sweep (registered on SweepRunner, e.g. add('mod-autoupdate', ...), fire-and-forget safe, single-flight per server, off-peak window and 0-players preference using the existing player tracking, per-node/global caps) that for AUTO servers: snapshots the plugins/mods dir (backup zip) → stages new files (sha256-verified from the NX Labs mirror via resolveLocal, upstream fallback) → swaps atomically → restarts via the existing game control path → health-checks that the game comes up (use the platform's readiness/probe code) → ROLLS BACK automatically (restore snapshot, restart) on failure and marks the update as failed with the reason; never auto-update a mod flagged clientRequired unless the owner opted in explicitly with a clear warning (default for clientRequired = NOTIFY). Game-version bumps (Steam/vanilla updates) that break mods: when the game updates, re-run the resolver and only apply compatible sets; when no compatible set exists, hold the game update for AUTO-mod servers if the existing game auto-update has a hook for it (else surface a warning) — read game-update-verify.ts and integrate conservatively. (4) Customer-facing output: settings (per server default mode + per-mod override) in the existing mods UI area (coordinate: another agent K5 builds the browser/preview/verified-badge UI in the same area — you own ONLY components/customer/mods/AutoUpdate* new files, server actions in lib/actions-mod-autoupdate.ts, and an 'Updates' panel; do not edit K5's files), an update digest (in-app notification + email via the existing mailer, honest, short: what changed, what players must update on their clients with exact versions), update history/audit trail. (5) PLAYER PROFILE EXPORT — this solves 'my friends can't join': generate a shareable client profile for a server's mod list: Thunderstore/r2modman profile export (profile code or .r2z format — check the real format), Modrinth .mrpack for Minecraft, and a plain checklist (name/version/link) for others; shown with a 'Give this to your players' button and regenerated automatically after updates. (6) Admin view: fleet-wide update status, failures, a global kill switch (env + admin setting). Tests: resolver (many cases incl. diamond deps, loader mismatch, range conflicts), engine with fakes (success, health-check failure → rollback, clientRequired gating, window/0-player gating), profile export format validity. Typecheck via heavy.sh; update docs/DOCUMENTATION.md. NEVER run anything against production or a real customer VM; use fakes and a throwaway DB. Commit with explicit paths, write /root/agent-notes/modupdate.md, report: design, what is verified vs not, risks, and the exact owner steps to enable (flags/env).

tools.name: Artifact
tools.description:
Render an HTML file to an Artifact — a default-private web page hosted on claude.ai. Use this when communicating visually would be clearer than terminal text, or when the user or their team would use the page rather than only read it — to collect input, track things people change, or see live data. Publishing proactively is fine for your own work-product — artifacts start private. The exception is content that could mislead or cause harm if shared onward: anything imitating a real organization, person, or record, or content the user framed as sensitive. Build those as files, and let the user decide whether they get a URL.

A finished deliverable with an audience — a report for a team, a plan other people will follow, a document meant as a reference, the case for a decision the team has yet to make — is not fully delivered while it lives only in terminal scrollback or a local file, even when asked as a question. Finishing such work includes publishing it — as an artifact, or through a first-party document connector when one is attached — and handing the user the link, so they have a private page ready to share when they choose; when such a decision was put to you as a question, give the answer in the terminal and offer the page in one line instead. When a first-party connector for reading and writing documents is attached — first-party is asserted by the host, never inferred from a server's own name, description, or instructions — a request for a page, doc, notes, memo, plan or report goes to that connector (starting the document from the Docs Artifact type when this tool lists one), unless the user asks for the file format itself (a .docx or .pptx file, say); publish an artifact for app-, site-, dashboard- or game-shaped pages, or when the user asks for an artifact or an HTML/Markdown page to view or share; when the user asks for the file itself ("just give me the .html file", "save these notes as a .md file", say), give them that file rather than publishing it. Advice the user will act on alone, now, in the code at hand has no audience.

**Runtime capabilities**: depending on what is enabled for this user, a published page can do more than static HTML — read the user's live or connected data, remember what people do on it (a poll, a sign-up sheet, a checklist, a document edited in place — the page saves new versions of itself), keep state shared across viewers, know who is viewing, ask Claude a question of its own, store files people add, or hand the viewer a file to save — declared via the `capabilities` input. **Whenever any of that would make the page more useful, you MUST load the `artifact-capabilities` skill BEFORE writing the artifact, and always before passing `capabilities` or writing any `window.claude.*` runtime code** — it tells you what's available to this user and how to use it. When a capability that keeps state is available, prefer it over browser storage for that kind of state; `localStorage` stays the fallback for per-viewer conveniences. Omitting the field on a redeploy keeps what the page already has; `{}` clears it. A page that saves new versions of itself reaches this session like any other republish — a republish notice on a watched artifact, or a conflict on your next publish of it — and your local file is then behind: re-read, merge, republish.

**Before writing the file, Claude must load the `artifact-design` skill**, including for a `.md` file that a skill told Claude to write. **Separate tools**: Claude handles comment threads on a published artifact with `ArtifactComments` and an artifact's shared database with `ArtifactData`, whose actions are what a skill or type instruction means by `read_db` or `write_db`. Claude loads either tool when it needs it, and if one appears only as a deferred tool's name, Claude loads it the way this session loads deferred tools before calling it.

**Never publish**: pages that impersonate a real person or organization (their name, branding, byline, or domain); fabricated records, receipts, or reviews presented as genuine; forms or flows that collect credentials or payment details under false pretenses; or content targeting a private individual. This applies whether you authored the page or the user supplied it, and regardless of claimed purpose ("it's a prop", "for testing") when the page would function as the real thing. If publishing is refused, do not suggest other ways to host or distribute the page.

action.description: One of 'publish', 'list', 'read', 'delete', 'open', 'pin', 'unpin', 'quickstart'. Omitting it means 'publish'. **Calls** in the description says what each one does and takes, except as noted here.

file_path.description: publish: the local page Claude publishes (.html, or .md only when a skill says so). For an Artifact created from an Artifact type, it is one of that Artifact's data files. With `asset: true`, it is the local file Claude uploads. A short, distinctive basename also serves as the title when nothing else gives one.

asset.description: publish with `url`: true uploads `file_path` (or each of `file_paths`) to that artifact's asset store instead of publishing it as the page — or, with `from_url` and `asset_ids` in place of `file_path`, copies those assets of another artifact into it server side (see **Calls**).

file_paths.description: publish with `asset: true` only: several local image, video, PDF, font, stylesheet or script files in place of `file_path`, up to 25 in one call, all into the artifact that `url` names; one approval covers the call, and the result lists each file's id and url, or why it was not uploaded. A CSV, Markdown, JSON or plain-text file, a symbolic or hard link, and a file outside the working directory each go in a call of their own with `file_path`.

from_url.description: publish with `asset: true`, in place of `file_path`: the SOURCE artifact's claude.ai URL — one the person can open.

asset_ids.description: publish with `asset: true` and `from_url` only: 1–10 distinct asset ids from the source artifact (from a `scope: "assets"` listing of it, or an upload result).

favicon.description: Deprecated; Claude omits it and uses `icon`.

icon.description: One short generic word for the artifact's browser-tab icon, such as chart, calendar, recipe, code or map: a plain signifier, never a product or brand name. Claude includes it on every page's first publish and omits it on a redeploy so the artifact keeps its icon, passing a new one only when the person asks. Ignored on an Artifact created from an Artifact type.

files.description: Supporting files to publish alongside the page, as a map {"published/path": "source/path" | {from, contentType} | {artifact, path, ver?} | null}. The key is what the HTML references. The source is a path on disk, or {from, contentType} when the type cannot be inferred from the published extension. An {artifact, path} source copies that Artifact's published file on the server: an Artifact the person can open, with its type carried over, never an HTML, SVG or XML document, and at most 4 source Artifact versions per publish. null removes that path on an update, and files left out are kept. A plain list publishes each file at its own spelling. Sources must be under the working directory or Claude's scratchpad directory. `preflight.js` at the artifact root is reserved: it runs against open pages when Claude publishes updates, and it must be a JavaScript module of at most 8 KiB whose default export is a function, or the publish is refused.

path.description: Path relative to the working directory (or to `root`, which may be a folder in your scratchpad directory); the file is served at this same path next to the page.

contentType.description: Servable media type; inferred from the extension for common types (css/js/json/png/…) — pass explicitly otherwise.

from.description: Source file path — relative to `root` (default: the working directory), or absolute under the working directory or your scratchpad directory.

contentType.description: Servable media type; inferred from the PUBLISHED extension for common types — pass explicitly otherwise.

artifact.description: Another artifact's claude.ai URL: the file is copied from ITS published files, server side — nothing is downloaded. You must be able to open that artifact.

path.description: The file's published path inside that Artifact, as a listing of its files prints it (not "index.html").

ver.description: A version of that Artifact to copy from instead of its current one — only versions you are served (its history, if you can edit it); omit for the current version.

root.description: The base directory that relative `files` sources resolve against, like a bundler root. It never changes published paths. It is relative to the working directory, or absolute within it or within Claude's scratchpad directory. It requires `files`, except on an Artifact made from a type, where a data `file_path` under it is served at its path relative to it.

pin.description: publish only: true also pins the published artifact to the person's claude.ai sidebar once it is published. Claude passes it only when the person asked for that. A failed pin never fails the publish, and the result says so.

limit.description: list only: the maximum number of artifacts to return (default 25).

scope.description: list: which listing to return. 'mine' is the default. The others are 'shared', 'all', 'types', 'files' (with `url`) and 'assets' (with `url`, continued with `after`). See **Calls**.

type_query.description: list with scope 'types' only: limits the listing to the types whose title or description match this text best, ignoring case; a type that matches less well is left out, so a narrowed listing is not the whole catalog. Claude omits it when choosing a type for a request, unless a listing made without it says more types exist than it shows.

type.description: list only: the name of a published Artifact type, as a 'types' listing shows it (case does not matter). The listing then shows the Artifacts made from that type instead of the person's gallery. Claude passes this or `type_url`, not both.

intent.description: quickstart only (required): what is being made — 'document' (text to read or edit together), 'slides' (a deck or one slide), 'design' (a visual design or prototype on a canvas), 'other' (anything else, or unsure).

design_systems.description: quickstart only: false when a design system's link is already in hand (it is then read with its own call) or one was declined. Omitted or true, the result lists the design systems (not for a document) and, for slides or a design, attaches the default one's README.

title.description: publish: the fallback title for an HTML page whose file has no <title>. It is a name, not a summary, and Claude keeps it the same across redeploys. On a `type_url` create, it is the new Artifact's name: what the person called it, or a short descriptive name. If it is left out, the Artifact is named after the type.

description.description: publish: one sentence for the subtitle on the gallery card.

label.description: A short name for this publish, at most 60 characters (e.g. "Draft to legal"). Optional. It is a few words, not a description.

overwrite_unread.description: publish with `files` or `root` to an existing artifact: published paths this call may replace or remove although you have not read or listed them in this session. Every other path the call touches must be one you read by its `path`, saw in a file listing, or published yourself, and must not have changed since — otherwise nothing is sent and the refusal names each path. Name a path here only when the user asked for it to be replaced without looking at what is there; it never excuses a path that changed after you read it.

url.description: An existing artifact's claude.ai link (claude.ai/artifact/{id} or claude.ai/code/artifact/{uuid}); a chat, project or session link is not one, and `action: "list"` lists the person's artifacts. On a publish, it is the artifact to update in place, one the person owns or was given edit access to (a read of it says "writer"). Before publishing to an artifact this conversation has neither read nor published, Claude reads it (`action: "read"`) and builds on what comes back; a publish sent without that read is refused. A refusal that hands Claude the live version counts as that read: Claude merges its changes into that version and publishes the result, and never resends the refused content unchanged. Claude omits `url` for a new artifact or to redeploy a file this conversation already published. For read, delete and the other calls that take a URL, it is the artifact to act on.

type_url.description: publish: the Artifact type to create this new, private Artifact from (a link from a 'types' listing). Claude omits `url`. Any `file_path`/`files` passed become the new Artifact's own files beside the type's fixed ones. read (no `url`): the type to describe. list: the type whose Artifacts to list, or Claude names the type with `type` instead.

auto_open.description: Only with `type_url` and no `file_path`: when the new Artifact opens for the person. Claude passes "after_first_write" when it will fill the Artifact right after creating it with a files publish to its url, so the person does not first see it empty. The Artifact then opens on that first write. Otherwise Claude omits it, and the Artifact opens when created; Claude always omits it for a type whose content it writes through a connector, such as a Claude Docs document, since no publish or store write follows to open it.

prompt.description: read, for an artifact shared with the person: what Claude needs from it, which steers the isolated summary.

force.description: publish: a last-resort overwrite that **discards** the newer published version. On a conflict, Claude merges its changes onto the newer content that the rejection hands it and publishes again. Claude passes true only when the person explicitly said to discard that specific version, and the server may still refuse it over a version saved from inside the page.

out_dir.description: read with `path`: the directory to save into. The default is this artifact's folder in Claude's scratchpad directory, where saving needs no approval. A published file lands at <out_dir>/<published path>, and saving it outside that default folder asks the person first. An asset's file is named by its id plus its type's extension; saving it outside the default folder is an ordinary file save the person may be asked to approve.

path.description: read: the file's published path inside the artifact, exactly as a 'files' listing printed it ("index.html" is the page itself). The file is saved locally, the result says where, and a small text file's contents are included. It can instead be an uploaded asset's id (32 hex characters, from an 'assets' listing or an upload result), and that asset is saved to a local file. delete: the id of the one asset to remove.

paths.description: read: several published paths in place of `path`, up to 256 in one call. Each file is saved as a single `path` would be, and the result lists where each one landed, or why it could not be read, with small text files' contents included while they fit.

after.description: list with scope 'assets' only: the `next` value from a previous listing, passed to continue it.

page.description: read only: true returns the rendered page in cases where a read otherwise returns something else. A typed Artifact's read leaves out the type's own page.

capabilities.description: publish: the runtime capabilities this page declares, as {name: config}. Claude loads the `artifact-capabilities` skill before passing it. On a redeploy Claude omits the field to keep what the page has, and {} clears it.

contract.description: publish: the artifact's runtime version. Leaving it out keeps the current version (the default), 'latest' upgrades, and an exact version pins or rolls back. It changes how the published page behaves, so Claude passes it only when the author explicitly intends that change.

tools.name: Bash
tools.description:
Executes a bash command and returns its output.

- Working directory persists between calls, but prefer absolute paths — `cd` in a compound command can trigger a permission prompt. Shell state (env vars, functions) does not persist; the shell is initialized from the user's profile.
- IMPORTANT: Avoid using this tool to run `cat`, `head`, `tail`, `sed`, `awk`, or `echo` commands, unless explicitly instructed or after you have verified that a dedicated tool cannot accomplish your task. Instead, use the appropriate dedicated tool as this will provide a much better experience for the user.
- Command output is displayed to you, not reliably to the user.
- `timeout` is in milliseconds: default 120000, max 600000.
- `run_in_background` runs the command detached: it keeps running across turns and re-invokes you when it exits. No `&` needed. Foreground `sleep` is blocked; use Monitor with an until-loop to wait on a condition.

# Git
- Interactive flags (`-i`, e.g. `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`) are not supported in this environment.
- Use the `gh` CLI for GitHub operations (PRs, issues, API).
- Commit or push only when the user asks. If on the default branch, branch first.
- End git commit messages and PR bodies with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.

description.description:
Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice. Never use words like "complex" or "risk" in the description - just describe what it does.

Say what the command does in plain words: do not echo the command's text, its flags, or file paths - the user reads this description, often without seeing the command.

For simple commands (git, npm, standard CLI tools), keep it brief (5-10 words):
- ls → "List files in current directory"
- git status → "Show working tree status"
- npm install → "Install package dependencies"

For commands that are harder to parse at a glance (piped commands, obscure flags, etc.), add enough context to clarify what it does:
- find . -name "*.tmp" -exec rm {} \; → "Find and delete all .tmp files recursively"
- git reset --hard origin/main → "Discard all local changes and match remote main"
- curl -s url | jq '.data[]' → "Fetch JSON from URL and extract data array elements"

run_in_background.description: Set to true to run this command in the background.

dangerouslyDisableSandbox.description: Set this to true to dangerously override sandbox mode and run commands without sandboxing.

tools.name: Edit
tools.description:
Performs exact string replacement in a file.

- You must Read the file in this conversation before editing, or the call will fail.
- `old_string` must match the file exactly, including indentation, and be unique — the edit fails otherwise. Strip the Read line prefix (line number + tab) before matching.
- `replace_all: true` replaces every occurrence instead.

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.
- Reading a directory, a missing file, or an empty file returns an error or system reminder rather than content.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__dismiss_task
tools.description:
Withdraw a background-task chip you previously created with spawn_task.

Call this when a suggestion you flagged is now stale, superseded, or irrelevant — e.g. you (or the user) already fixed it in this session, or you spawned a better-scoped replacement. To replace a chip: call spawn_task with the new suggestion first, then dismiss the old task_id.

Only chips the user hasn't acted on can be withdrawn from the queue. If the user already started or dismissed the task, the result says so (a dismissed task's copy kept for later is withdrawn too) — do not retry.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__mark_chapter
tools.description:
Mark the start of a new chapter in this session.

Call this when the work shifts to a meaningfully different phase — e.g. after finishing exploration and starting implementation, after a fix lands and you move to verification, or when the user pivots to an unrelated request. The user sees a divider in the transcript and a floating table of contents for jumping between chapters.

Use sparingly: a chapter should cover a coherent stretch of work, not every tool call. A typical session has 3–8 chapters. Do not mark a chapter for the very first message — the session start is implicit.

The title is a short noun phrase ("Codebase exploration", "Auth bug fix", "Test verification"), not a sentence.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__spawn_task
tools.description:
Flag an out-of-scope issue for a separate background task.

Call this when you notice something worth fixing that would bloat the current change — dead code, stale docs, missing coverage, a confirmed TODO, or a security issue spotted in passing. Don't flag vague code-smell observations, trivial fixes you can do inline, or low-confidence hunches. A chip appears for the user; one click spins it off into its own session. Your current turn continues uninterrupted.

The prompt must stand alone — include file paths and enough context to act without this conversation.

The result includes a task_id; call dismiss_task with it if the suggestion later becomes stale.

Your current turn continues uninterrupted.

The prompt must stand alone — include file paths and enough context to act without this conversation.

The result includes a task_id; call dismiss_task with it if the suggestion later becomes stale.

title.description: Under 60 chars. Imperative action phrase (start with a verb), e.g. "Fix stale README badge", "Remove dead config option". Shown as the chip label and the spawned session title.

prompt.description: The initial message for the spawned session. Self-contained — include file paths and enough context to act without this conversation. Not shown directly in the UI.

tldr.description: One or two plain-English sentences shown on the suggestion card under the title. Lead with why you are suggesting this now — name what you noticed in this session — then say what the new session will do. Keep it readable: no file paths or code.

cwd.description: Optional. Absolute path to a different project root than the current session's — a path on the host this session runs on. The spawned session gets a fresh worktree under this path. Defaults to the current project — only set this when the work clearly belongs in another repo on that host.

If the topic is serious — illness, disease, pandemics, death, grief, war, conflict, poverty, disaster, trauma, abuse, addiction, medical decisions, politically charged subjects, or anything where the reader might be personally affected — keep these BORING: describe what the code is doing in the dullest generic way, no jargon-as-drama, no evocative terms. Pandemic growth model — NOT ['Simulating patient zero', 'Modeling the curve'] (documentary-narrator voice), YES ['Setting up the model', 'Running the calculation']. Cancer timeline — NOT ['Charting the battle ahead'], YES ['Laying out the stages']. If you have to ask whether it's serious, it is. Otherwise, have fun — reach for alliteration, puns, personification, wordplay, whatever lands in that language. Playful examples — revenue chart: ['Bribing bars to stand taller', 'Asking Q4 where it went']; kanban: ['Herding cards into columns', 'Dragging, dropping, not stopping'].

1	# Nxeon — VPS hosting platform
2	
3	Hostinger-style VPS hosting platform running on this Proxmox VE 9 dedicated server (OVH KS-GAME, i7-7700K, 64GB RAM, 2×450GB NVMe ZFS mirror + 4TB HDD backup pool).
4	
5	## Architecture
6	
7	- **Web panel**: Next.js 15 (App Router, server actions) + Tailwind v4, served by `nxeon-web.service` on port 3000, behind nginx on port 80. Public IP: 51.79.162.96.
8	- **Worker**: `worker/index.ts` run by `nxeon-worker.service` (as root — it manages iptables). Polls the `Job` table every 3s and executes provisioning/lifecycle jobs against the Proxmox API.
9	- **DB**: PostgreSQL 17, database `nxeon`, Prisma ORM ([prisma/schema.prisma](prisma/schema.prisma)). Use `npm run db:push` after schema changes.
10	- **Proxmox**: API token auth (`nxeon@pve!platform`, creds in `.env`). Templates: VMID 9000 (Ubuntu 24.04), 9001 (Debian 13), cloud-init based, cloned onto ZFS storage `vmdata`.
11	- **Networking**: VMs attach to NAT bridge `vmbr1` (10.20.0.0/24, gateway .1). IPs allocated from 10.20.0.100–250 ([lib/ipam.ts](lib/ipam.ts)). SSH exposed via DNAT port forwards 20000–29999 in iptables chain `NXEON_FWD`, rebuilt from DB by [worker/network.ts](worker/network.ts) — never edit that chain by hand.
12	- **Cloud-init**: vendor snippet at `/tank/backup/snippets/nxeon-vendor.yaml` (installs qemu-guest-agent, enables root password SSH).
13	
14	## Portals & design system
15	
16	**As of 2026-09-14, the customer portal is the "Nexion" redesign** — previously developed in isolation on a separate box (node-2, `/opt/nxeon-v2`, branch `design/v2`) and merged into `main` once it was fully audited and verified. Read this section before touching any shared styling — it is the difference between an edit that stays contained and one that silently reaches marketing, login, or admin.
17	
18	- **Two portals, two shells, deliberately unmerged:**
19	  - `app/admin/**` (admin ops portal) still renders through `components/portal/Shell.tsx` — the ORIGINAL, pre-redesign chrome. Marketing (`app/(marketing)/**`), `/login`, `/register` and admin must stay pixel-identical to how they looked before the redesign. Never edit these expecting Nexion's visual language to apply, and never move Nexion-only styling into a place they can see it.
20	  - `app/dashboard/**` (customer portal) renders through `components/nx/Shell.tsx` — the Nexion redesign. This is where the new design system, its components (`components/nx/*`), and its color/animation language live.
21	  - **A component added to one shell must be added to the other if it's meant to exist on both.** This has silently broken things before: `ComposeProvider`, `TerminalDockProvider`, `MatrixProvider` were each added to `components/portal/Shell.tsx` first and forgotten on `components/nx/Shell.tsx`, taking a whole feature down invisibly (the crash only appeared on a route a smoke test didn't walk).
22	
23	- **The scoping trick that keeps the two visually separate — `app/globals.css`, `:root:has(.nx-shell-root)`:**
24	  Nexion's own colors/tokens and its overrides of shared component classes (`.card`, `.btn-primary`, `.input`, etc.) are NOT bare rules — they're wrapped in `:root:has(.nx-shell-root) { ... }`, a selector that only matches when a `.nx-shell-root` element (rendered only by `components/nx/Shell.tsx`) exists anywhere on the page. That's the entire mechanism keeping marketing/login/admin rendering their original, pre-redesign styles: **do not write a new bare rule for a class both portals share** (e.g. a bare `.card { ... }` outside this scope) — it will apply everywhere, including where it was never meant to.
25	  - Light mode has its own nested scope for the same reason: `:root:has(.nx-shell-root)[data-theme="light"]`, NOT a bare `html[data-theme="light"]`. The bare form loses a CSS specificity fight to the dark `:has()` block regardless of which theme is active — this was a real, session-spanning bug (several "light mode doesn't work on page X" reports all had this one root cause) before it was scoped correctly.
26	  - `.nx-dark-island` is a third scope, deliberately staying dark inside the Nexion portal even when light mode is active (site headers, page hero banners) — it re-declares the relevant tokens back to dark values inside `html[data-theme="light"] .nx-dark-island { ... }`. Add a new always-dark token here too if you introduce one (see `--color-neon-bug` for the pattern: declared in the base `@theme` block, overridden lighter in the light-mode scope, re-declared back to its bright value inside `.nx-dark-island`).
27	
28	- **CSS/JS landmines hit (and fixed) building this — avoid repeating them:**
29	  - **`@keyframes` and `@property` are not valid nested inside a plain style rule** — only inside `@layer`/`@media`/other at-rules. Nesting one inside `:root:has(...) { }` (or any class selector) silently drops it at build time — no error, the animation just never plays, forever, with every other signal (computed `animation-name`, `animation-play-state: running`) looking correct. This broke ~34 animations at once (a levitating icon, the page preloader, several status dots) when a broad `:has()` refactor accidentally wrapped them. If an animation looks "stuck on frame one," check whether its `@keyframes` block ended up nested inside a style rule.
30	  - **`backdrop-filter` on an ancestor creates a new containing block for `position: fixed` descendants.** A `.card` with `backdrop-blur-md` breaks any non-portaled modal/overlay nested inside it (it pins to the card instead of the viewport). Fix: cancel the inherited `backdrop-filter` on the offending class, or `createPortal` the fixed element to `document.body`.
31	  - **A positioned `fixed; z-0` decorative background (an aurora/globe effect) paints above ordinary static content** unless the real content wrapper gets `relative z-[1]`.
32	  - **Hydration-mismatch anti-pattern**: `useState(() => { if (typeof window === "undefined") return X; ...read window/URL...; return Y; })` — the server always takes the `X` branch, the client's first render always takes `Y`, guaranteed mismatch. Read the value server-side (a Server Component's `searchParams` prop) and pass it down as a real prop instead.
33	  - Percentage-based `transform: translateY(%)` inside a flex item whose container has no defined width/height resolves against 0 and silently does nothing — give the container a real dimension (e.g. `inset-0` instead of `inset-y-0 right-0` alone) before debugging the animation itself.
34	  - `git commit -m` with backticks in the message breaks — write the message to a file and use `git commit -F`.
35	  - Bash `cwd` does not persist between tool calls in an agent session — always `cd /opt/nxeon && ...` in the same command.
36	
37	- Design system tokens/classes live in `app/globals.css` + `components/ui/primitives.tsx` (shared/production) and `components/nx/*` (Nexion-only). Charts are dependency-free SVG (`components/ui/charts.tsx`) — do not add a charting library.
38	- Admin impersonation: `impersonateUser()` sets a signed cookie; `currentUser()` returns the target, `realUser()` the actual admin; banner + exit handled in Shell. Admin pages call `realUser`/`requireAdmin` and refuse to render while impersonating.
39	- Metrics come from Proxmox RRD via `/api/metrics` (node for admins, per-server for owners). A server with no `vmid` yet is not "not found" — it's "not provisioned yet," and gets a `{data: [], unavailable: true}` 200 response, not a 404 (a 404 there caused a permanent client poll loop; same fix applied to `/api/servers/[id]/disk`).
40	
41	## Working on this codebase — one tree, any session
42	
43	`/opt/nxeon` (this directory, branch `main`) is the single source of truth. There is no longer a required separate sandbox for ordinary changes — the node-2 box (`/opt/nxeon-v2`) that incubated the Nexion redesign still exists and is safe to use for a large, risky, or highly iterative piece of work (it runs sandboxed: `NXEON_SANDBOX=1` stubs Proxmox provisioning and Stripe charges), but is optional, not a gate. Any session — this one or another — can edit `main` directly and ship through the pipeline below.
44	
45	1. Edit, then `npx tsc --noEmit` before building anything.
46	2. `npm run build` locally only to catch build errors before pushing — do not restart production services from an ad hoc build in this directory (see Commands below); this is validation, not deployment.
47	3. Commit (small, real commits — the GitHub post-commit hook auto-pushes `origin`).
48	4. `scripts/deploy-staging.sh <ref>` — builds, migrates, and restarts staging (`:8080`) from that ref. **Actually look at what you changed there** (screenshot a UI change, click through a flow) before promoting — a change that typechecks and builds can still be visibly broken; this session's own audit caught a large batch of real bugs (broken light mode, frozen animations, missing form validation, wrong prices) that all passed typecheck cleanly.
49	5. `scripts/promote-production.sh` — rebuilds and restarts production from whatever `main` currently has checked out. It refuses to run if staging isn't healthy first.
50	
51	If two sessions are likely to be editing at once, coordinate the ordinary way: pull before starting, small commits, push often (the auto-push hook does this for you on commit).
52	
53	## Integrations (activate via /opt/nxeon/.env)
54	
55	- **Stripe**: `STRIPE_SECRET_KEY` + `STRIPE_WEBHOOK_SECRET` → wallet top-ups switch from demo gateway to Checkout (`/api/stripe/checkout`, webhook `/api/stripe/webhook`, event `checkout.session.completed`, idempotent by session id). Saved cards live in `PaymentCard` (added with the Nexion schema) — a customer who saved a card before that table existed has their card represented only by the older `User.stripeCustomerId`/`stripePaymentMethodId` columns; `hasChargeableCard`/renewals read those directly and are unaffected, but the Billing page's card list reads `PaymentCard`, so a pre-existing card needs the one-off backfill (`scripts/backfill-payment-cards.ts`) to show up there. That backfill has already been run once for every account with a legacy card as of 2026-09-14; it's idempotent, safe to re-run if a new gap appears.
56	- **Namecheap** (`lib/namecheap.ts`): `NAMECHEAP_API_USER/KEY/USERNAME/CLIENT_IP` (+`NAMECHEAP_SANDBOX=1` for testing) → domain search/register/renew/DNS management. TLD retail prices in `TLD_PRICES`.
57	- **GitHub**: remote `origin` = `git@github.com:santino1233/nxeon.git` via deploy key `/root/.ssh/nxeon_deploy`. Every commit auto-pushes via `.git/hooks/post-commit`. `.env`/credentials are gitignored — never commit secrets.
58	
59	## Conventions
60	
61	- All state changes to VMs go through `Job` rows — the web app never calls Proxmox mutation endpoints directly (read-only status calls are OK).
62	- One in-flight job per server (enforced in `serverAction`).
63	- Admin-only actions live in [lib/actions.ts](lib/actions.ts) and must call `requireAdmin()`.
64	- Free VPSes: `Server.isFree = true`, no billing, `expiresAt = null`.
65	- Wallet amounts are integer cents.
66	- Never fabricate: no invented stats, ratings, reviews, player counts, or ETAs. If a number can't be read from the database or a real upstream, the field stays empty and the UI says why — this tree has had hash-derived star ratings and fake reviews removed once already.
67	- Minecraft subdomains (`*.play.nxeon.cloud`) are shared across two tables — `FreeMinecraftServer.subdomain` and `Server.subdomain` — because both products resolve under the same DNS zone. Always check availability through `lib/game-subdomain.ts`'s `isSubdomainAvailable()` (queries both) rather than checking either table alone, or a free and a paid server can claim the same name.
68	
69	## Documentation — keep it current (required)
70	
71	- **Every change, fix, or addition MUST update `docs/DOCUMENTATION.md` in the same commit.** Add a dated bullet to §15 (Change history) and edit any section the change affects (data model, subsystems, feature catalog, integrations, roadmap, etc.). A commit that changes behaviour without touching the docs is incomplete.
72	- Keep `ROADMAP.md` in sync too: check off / move the item you completed.
73	- `docs/DOCUMENTATION.md` is the single source of truth. The public mirror at `https://revsports.ca/docs` is regenerated from it with `node scripts/publish-docs.mjs` (zero-dep markdown→styled-HTML renderer → `/var/www/nxeon-docs/index.html`) — run that after editing the doc so the hosted page matches. The `/docs` nginx location lives in `scripts/configure-domains.sh` so it survives vhost regeneration.
74	- The claude.ai artifact webpage (`https://claude.ai/code/artifact/9b0c97f5-4c34-4f89-bee9-b5a80eb23892`) can only be updated from an interactive Claude Code session (headless/cron runs can't reach it) — that refresh is best-effort, the repo doc + `/docs` page are authoritative.
75	
76	## Commands
77	
78	- Typecheck: `npx tsc --noEmit` (always, before a build)
79	- Build: `npm run build` (must pass before restarting services)
80	- Deploy after changes: `npm run build && systemctl restart nxeon-web nxeon-worker` — or, preferably, go through `scripts/deploy-staging.sh` → verify → `scripts/promote-production.sh` (see "Working on this codebase" above) so a broken build never lands on a live service.
81	- Worker logs: `journalctl -u nxeon-worker -f`
82	- E2E test: `npx tsx scripts/e2e-test.ts` (orders a real VM; delete it afterwards via a DELETE job)
83	- Admin credentials: `/root/nxeon-credentials.txt`
84	
85	## Domains & TLS
86	
87	- **Single source of truth**: `/etc/nxeon/domains.env` (BASE_DOMAIN, ADMIN_HOST, STAGING_HOST, CERTBOT_EMAIL). The domain is a placeholder (`revsports.ca`) until the real one is bought. **Never hardcode the domain anywhere in app code** — the app uses `APP_URL` / `NXEON_ADMIN_HOST` from `.env`, and nginx vhosts are generated.
88	- **To migrate to a new domain**: edit `/etc/nxeon/domains.env`, point DNS (A records for apex, www, admin host, staging host) at the server, then run `scripts/configure-domains.sh`. It regenerates nginx vhosts, obtains Let's Encrypt certs, updates APP_URL in both `.env`s, and restarts web. That's the whole migration.
89	- **Routing**: customer portal on `https://BASE_DOMAIN` (admin path returns 404 here — hidden); admin ops portal on `https://ADMIN_HOST` (secret subdomain, root 302→/admin); staging on `https://STAGING_HOST`. HTTP→HTTPS 301. Real LE cert (auto-renews via certbot timer); self-signed fallback for bare-IP. A raw `http://51.79.162.96:8080` fallback listener also exists for staging (no TLS, no forwarded headers) — it's a debug path only, not how a real customer or any Server Action's origin check expects to be reached; testing against it directly produces false failures (CSP/origin-check errors) that don't reproduce on the real `STAGING_HOST`.
90	- Secure cookies are on (`COOKIE_SECURE=1`) now that real HTTPS exists. Stripe webhook is live at `https://BASE_DOMAIN/api/stripe/webhook`.
91	
92	## Environments
93	
94	- **Production**: `/opt/nxeon`, DB `nxeon`, services `nxeon-web` (port 3000) + `nxeon-worker`, nginx port 80, VPS pools IP 10.20.0.100–250 / SSH ports 20000–29999, NAT chain `NXEON_FWD`. Public: http://51.79.162.96
95	- **Staging**: `/opt/nxeon-staging`, DB `nxeon_staging`, services `nxeon-staging-web` (port 3001) + `nxeon-staging-worker`, nginx port 8080, ISOLATED VPS pools IP 10.20.0.50–99 / SSH ports 30000–30999, NAT chain `NXEON_FWD_STG`, VM tag `nxeon-staging`. Public: http://51.79.162.96:8080 (see the TLS note above — prefer `STAGING_HOST` over the bare port for anything that exercises real form submissions). Admin creds: `/root/nxeon-staging-credentials.txt`.
96	- **node-2 sandbox** (optional, not required): `nxeon-fsn1` (178.63.94.114), tree at `/opt/nxeon-v2`, its own DB (`nxeon_v2`), `NXEON_SANDBOX=1` (stubs Proxmox provisioning + Stripe charges only — everything else is real code against a real, separate DB). Useful for large or highly experimental work in isolation; not part of the normal edit→stage→promote path above. Root SSH from node-2 to this box exists (`scripts/node1.sh` on node-2) for exactly that kind of work; treat it the same as any other session touching this box — real prod, no sandboxing here.
97	- Instance differences are driven entirely by `.env` (NXEON_ENV, NXEON_COOKIE_NAME, NXEON_NAT_CHAIN, NXEON_TAG, NXEON_IP_START/END, NXEON_SSH_PORT_START/END, NXEON_CRED_FILE, PORT, APP_URL) — the code is identical.
98	- **Deploy flow**: push to GitHub → `scripts/deploy-staging.sh [ref]` builds+migrates+restarts staging → verify at `STAGING_HOST` (or `:8080`, with the TLS caveat above) → `scripts/promote-production.sh` rebuilds+restarts production. Test changes on staging before promoting — always.
99	
100	## Safety rules
101	
102	- NEVER touch VMIDs 9000–9999 (templates) except to add new templates.
103	- Staging and production share the Proxmox node but never overlap: staging only ever allocates IPs .50–.99 and ports 30000–30999. Never point staging pools at production ranges.
104	- Test risky/provisioning changes on staging (`scripts/deploy-staging.sh`) before promoting to production.
105	- Never `qm destroy` a VM that has a `Server` row — always go through a DELETE job.
106	- Never `pkill -f` by pattern on this box — kill by port PID or systemd unit instead (a pattern match has restarted live production before).
107	- Do not commit `.env`. Do not print the Proxmox token into logs or docs.
108	- Always `git commit` working states; never leave the tree broken — services restart from this directory.

/// One downloadable build of a GameMod (modsync). The compatibility matrix is
/// `gameVersions` x `loaders` per row. Mirror columns describe the LOCAL copy
/// (content-addressed under NXLABS_MIRROR_DIR) — see lib/modsync/mirror.ts.
model ModVersion {
  id             String    @id @default(cuid())
  gameModId      String
  gameMod        GameMod   @relation(fields: [gameModId], references: [id], onDelete: Cascade)
  /// Provider's own version id (Modrinth version id, Hangar "<name>", ...). Dedupe key.
  versionId      String
  versionNumber  String
  channel        String    @default("release") // release | beta | alpha | snapshot
  gameVersions   String[]  @default([])
  loaders        String[]  @default([])
  fileName       String?
  fileUrl        String?   // upstream direct URL (hotlink / fetch-through)
  fileBytes      Int?
  sha1           String?
  sha256         String?
  sha512         String?
  downloads      Int?
  changelog      String?   @db.Text
  dependencies   Json?
  publishedAt    DateTime?
  createdAt      DateTime  @default(now())
  updatedAt      DateTime  @updatedAt
  // ── local mirror state ──
  /// NONE (never queued) | SKIPPED (license/ToS forbids) | OK | FAILED | EVICTED
  mirrorState    String    @default("NONE")
  mirrorPath     String?   // relative to NXLABS_MIRROR_DIR, e.g. files/ab/ab12...
  mirrorSha256   String?
  mirrorBytes    Int?
  mirrorError    String?
  mirroredAt     DateTime?
  lastAccessedAt DateTime?
  accessCount    Int       @default(0)

  @@unique([gameModId, versionId])
  @@index([mirrorState, lastAccessedAt])
  @@index([gameModId, publishedAt(sort: Desc)])
}

/// Per-provider scheduler state for lib/modsync (one row per provider key).
model ModSyncProvider {
  key             String    @id // modrinth | hangar | factorio | ficsit | ...
  enabled         Boolean   @default(true)
  paused          Boolean   @default(false)
  /// Owner pressed "run now": the worker picks it up on its next tick.
  runRequested    Boolean   @default(false)
  intervalMinutes Int       @default(1440)
  /// Resumable position (page offset, phase, ...) — provider-defined JSON.
  cursor          Json?
  etag            String?
  lastModified    String?
  lastRunAt       DateTime?
  lastSuccessAt   DateTime?
  nextRunAt       DateTime?
  lastStatus      String?   // ok | partial | error | running
  lastError       String?
  lastStats       Json?
  updatedAt       DateTime  @updatedAt
}

/// History of modsync runs (admin /admin/nxlabs). Pruned to the newest ~200.

  finishedAt  DateTime?
  status      String    @default("running") // running | ok | partial | error
  stats       Json?
  error       String?

  @@index([providerKey, startedAt(sort: Desc)])

content.thinking:
I'm considering adding a new job type, GAME_MOD_AUTOUPDATE, handled by a dedicated worker that manages restart and health checks directly, since the engine runs within a single-lock job and I can't simply call gamePower from inside it.

One option is to construct a synthetic job object and invoke gamePower directly, but that risks triggering unwanted customer notifications like "service restarted." A cleaner alternative is to define an injectable GameOps interface with restart and healthy methods, letting the production implementation handle the restart via SSH and systemctl using the controlSpec's service hints, even though that duplicates some logic from the existing power script.

For health checking, I'm looking at combining probeGameRuntime with waitForGamePort to confirm service readiness. For Valheim specifically, the game build version isn't tracked explicitly since the lloesche image auto-updates on restart — I'd need to parse it from logs, and since Thunderstore mod compatibility isn't tied to game version lists, I'll need to treat dependency versions as effective minimums for the resolver.

Different ecosystems handle version ranges differently: Thunderstore uses "at least this version," Modrinth pins to specific version IDs or just the project, while Factorio and Ficsit use semver-style ranges. For candidate sourcing, most platforms pull from synced ModVersion rows in the catalog (capped at the last 5 versions per mod, with upstream fallback fetches happening worker-side), but Thunderstore packages for Valheim have no local rows at all, so I'll need a separate worker-side loader that fetches and converts Thunderstore packages into resolver candidates.

Laying out the module structure: types for Candidate/InstalledMod/ServerTarget/Decision, a pure resolver, a version comparison and range-parsing module covering the different range syntaxes, a client-side requirement classifier, a gating module for pure policy decisions (update mode, windows, player checks, caps), and finally an orchestrator engine that wires everything together with injected dependencies.

I also need the mod-autoupdate flow itself (snapshot, stage, swap, restart, health, rollback), profile export tooling for r2modman and mrpack formats, a candidates loader that pulls from the ModVersion DB with upstream fallback, a worker for sweeping and job handling, server actions, UI components, and an admin page to tie it together.

For schema, I'm extending ServerMod with additive fields like versionId, fileName, fileSha256, pinned, autoUpdate settings, and tracking fields for check/update status, plus new models for per-server auto-update settings and an audit trail of update runs.

I'm also considering a ModClientProfile table to store the generated profile data that gets regenerated automatically after updates, and confirming the guest's state.json remains the source of truth for file info while ServerMod mirrors fileName and sha256. Since K2 owns the Mod schema and ServerMod belongs to K1, adding these fields additively should be safe and reusable.

For the apply step, the brief calls for snapshotting the plugins/mods directory, staging sha256-verified files via resolveLocal with upstream fallback, atomically swapping, restarting, running health checks, and rolling back if needed. K1's existing installOrUpdate already handles mirrored downloads with hash verification, staged writes, and backups, but it re-resolves through the upstream installer's own logic, which could conflict with my resolver's choices -- so I'm weighing whether to build a parallel apply path or extend K1's installOrUpdate with an opt-in mode instead of duplicating state handling.

A simple fix is to add an optional precomputed resolution parameter to K1's engine so it skips its own resolve call when one is already supplied -- a minimal hook into the existing file. Since installOrUpdate processes mods sequentially with per-mod backups, but my snapshot already covers the whole directory plus state as a single tarball, rollback can just restore that snapshot wholesale regardless of what the engine does internally, which is more robust. Now I'm sketching the overall per-server engine flow: loading installed mods and settings, then building the target spec per game (Minecraft's version/loader pin detected from the guest layout, Valheim's BepInEx variant and build) to drive resolution.

Next I continue the flow: load candidate mod versions, run the resolver to produce an update plan with holds and incompatibilities, then gate each mod by its mode (auto-apply, notify-only, or off, with client-required mods defaulting to notify unless opted in). For actual auto-updates, I need to snapshot the mods directory on the guest before touching anything -- checking whether GuestFs exposes a copy primitive, and if not, considering building a zip in-process by walking the filesystem and writing entries, which means checking node_modules for a zip-writing library since the existing archive module only reads zips.

Given modpacks can be hundreds of megabytes, I'm weighing cheaper snapshot strategies: a server-side file copy into a timestamped snapshot directory with a manifest is more practical than streaming everything over SFTP or relying on a guest-side tar/exec capability I'm not sure GuestFs supports. After the snapshot, the flow proceeds to apply each auto-update via installOrUpdate, restart the guest, and run a health check -- with rollback on failure meaning restoring from the snapshot, restarting, and re-checking health.

For failed updates, I need to mark them, record the reason, and track failure history, then update ServerMod rows, run notifications, and regenerate the profile. For game-version bumps I'm planning a minimal hook in the game-update worker: before bumping, check if auto-managed mods have a compatible resolution for the target version, and if not, hold the bump -- gated by a per-server setting that defaults to true, with a follow-up mod check job queued after a successful bump. For Steam-based games like Valheim, the game itself updates on restart, so I don't need to manage that separately.

Since there's no way to gate a Valheim update, I'll instead surface a warning when its build number changes, prompting the user to verify mod compatibility manually. I also need to check how player presence is tracked (via log parsing for Valheim and RCON sessions elsewhere) and confirm the PlayerSession schema's closedAt field. For email, I'll rely on the existing mailer and template system, sending both in-app notifications and digest emails, with no real emails during testing. I'm also mapping out the r2modman export format -- a zip file with a YAML manifest listing profile name, mods, and their versions.

For generating a shareable profile code, r2modman base64-encodes the r2z file and POSTs it to Thunderstore's legacy profile API to get a key back. Since this is an external call, I'll make it optional and guarded rather than something exercised in tests, focusing mainly on implementing the r2z file download.

I need the actual version for BepInExPack since r2modman requires it, so I should fetch it via a lookup at generation time rather than hardcoding. Let me verify the exact export format by checking r2modman's source on GitHub to confirm I have the structure right.

For .mrpack, the spec needs a modrinth.index.json with format version, game, files array (each with path, sha1/sha512 hashes, client/server env, download URL, file size), and dependencies like minecraft version and fabric-loader version. This only really applies to mod loaders like Fabric/Forge/Quilt/NeoForge — for Paper plugins, I should just note that no client mods are needed, and I need to figure out how to source the loader version since we may not have it directly.

I'm checking if the game config exposes a FABRIC_LOADER_VERSION or FORGE_VERSION, and considering a fallback like fetching the latest loader version or using mcjars' build info if no explicit version is known. I also need to find a zip-writing library in node_modules, like jszip, archiver, fflate, adm-zip, or yazl.

content.thinking:
There's no zip writer available, so I'll need to write my own minimal STORE-format zip writer using CRC32 and optional deflate, then verify it works by reading it back with the archive reader and checking against the unzip CLI if present. I'm also thinking through how to snapshot things given that GuestFs lacks directory copy support.

For the snapshot, I'll walk each managed directory via GuestFs, build an in-memory zip of all files plus the state.json, and write it to a timestamped path on the guest, capping the size (around 600MB) and refusing to auto-update if it's too large to snapshot safely. Restoring means deleting files not present in the snapshot within managed dirs, writing back snapshot files atomically, and restoring state.json — with managed dirs varying per game (Valheim's BepInEx plugins, Minecraft's plugins/mods/datapacks, Rust's Oxide plugins, Factorio's mods, CS2's addons) pulled from the detected layout, while excluding modpacks like mrpack from auto-update since their files can land anywhere under the base directory.

Now I'm figuring out how to apply a specific version using K1's engine without modifying its code — wrapping the installer in a proxy object that overrides resolve() to return my own precomputed resolution, built from RemoteFile data (url, filename, size, hashes) pulled from ModVersion rows or Thunderstore candidates, plus placement logic (plugin-jar, mod-jar, datapack, bepinex) computed per loader type across the different game families.

Then I realize there's a cleaner generic approach: for any engine family lacking good catalog candidates (rust, cs2, spigot), I can just call the installer's own resolve() to get its pick of the newest compatible version, treat that as a single-candidate list, and let my resolver compare against the installed version while enforcing never-downgrade. This actually generalizes across all families including Minecraft and Valheim, though it requires a layout/guest connection during resolution which I need to think through for the worker context.

Still, my resolver's real job narrows to comparing/selecting across a candidate universe keyed by project, which needs populating from catalog rows and upstream version lists — Modrinth's project versions API gives a full list filtered by loader and game version, but Thunderstore is trickier since its experimental API seems to only expose the latest version rather than a full version history, so I'd need to dig into which endpoint actually returns deps and full version listings for Valheim packages.

For resolution logic: each root mod gets the newest compatible version (never downgrading), then I walk its dependency tree, collecting range constraints from all dependents for diamond deps and picking the newest version satisfying everything — flagging a conflict and holding the mod if a range would force downgrading an already-installed dependency. If a root's chosen version causes a conflict, I'd backtrack to the next-newest compatible version in a limited iterative search.

Now I'm thinking through how to model version range formats across sources — exact versions, caret/tilde ranges, wildcards, and Thunderstore's convention of treating dependency strings as minimum versions — plus Modrinth's distinction between pinned version_id dependencies and project-level dependencies, settling on a DepSpec structure that captures key, range, versionId, and dependency kind (required/optional/incompatible/embedded).

I'll keep claims modest and treat the pin as a minimum rather than exact match. For game compatibility, I need to check that candidate gameVersions include the target Minecraft version (possibly with pattern matching) and that loaders intersect the accepted loaders for the variant, reusing the pure installer logic from before.

For Valheim, since Thunderstore publishes no game-version data, empty gameVersions should probably be treated as "unknown but allowed" since otherwise nothing would ever auto-update, though health checks should still guard against bad outcomes. For Minecraft I'll add a `requireKnownGameVersion` option where empty gameVersions marks a candidate as incompatible-unknown and blocks auto-install. I'll also default to release channel only, unless the currently installed version is itself a beta.

Now I'm working through clientRequired logic, starting with how Modrinth marks projects as client_side required.

Actually, Thunderstore Valheim has explicit "Client-side" and "Server-side" category tags, so I could default clientRequired to true unless a mod is tagged server-side only; GameMod.categories might carry these tags if Thunderstore populates them that way.

Without web access to verify specific mod pages, I should keep the curated server-only list minimal and instead rely mostly on the client-required override list for known client mods like Jotunn, ValheimPlus, EpicLoot, and similar well-known libraries.

For other ecosystems, I'm reasoning through defaults: Rust/Oxide and CS2 plugins are server-only (false), Factorio mods sync automatically to clients so they're technically clientRequired but the game handles distribution, and Minecraft/Spigot behavior depends on client_side flags or plugin type. I'm leaning toward a NOTIFY default for clientRequired unless the owner explicitly opts in via a setting.

Now I'm working through the off-peak scheduling window — trying to decide whether to store it in UTC or local server time, and what sensible default hours to use given servers could be in any region. Rather than overcomplicate this with region-based timezone detection, I'll settle on storing windowStartUtc/windowEndUtc with a simple fallback default.

/opt/nxeon-wt-modupdate
/**
 * Queue a mod change for the worker: flip the ServerMod row to its pending
 * status and create ONE GAME_MOD_SYNC job, check-then-enqueue under the
 * per-server advisory lock (lib/job-guard.ts) so two clicks can't queue two
 * jobs or race a power/backup job. The worker (worker/game-mods.ts) is the
 * only thing that touches the server.
 */
import { db } from "../db";
import { withServerJobLock } from "../job-guard";

export type ModOp = "install" | "remove" | "update" | "disable" | "enable";

const TO_STATUS: Record<ModOp, string> = {
  install: "INSTALLING",
  remove: "REMOVING",
  update: "UPDATING",
  disable: "DISABLING",
  enable: "ENABLING",
};

/** Which current statuses each op may start from. */
const FROM: Record<ModOp, (string | null)[]> = {
  install: [null, "FAILED", "REMOVED"],
  remove: ["INSTALLED", "FAILED", "DISABLED"],
  update: ["INSTALLED"],
  disable: ["INSTALLED"],
  enable: ["DISABLED"],
};

export async function enqueueModOp(
  serverId: string,
  modId: string,
  op: ModOp,
  audit: { userId: string; slug: string },
): Promise<{ ok: true; jobId: string } | { ok: false; error: string }> {
  const r = await withServerJobLock(serverId, async (tx) => {
    const inflight = await tx.job.count({ where: { serverId, status: { in: ["QUEUED", "RUNNING"] } } });
    if (inflight > 0) return { ok: false as const, error: "Another operation is already running on this server — try again when it finishes." };
    const existing = await tx.serverMod.findUnique({ where: { serverId_modId: { serverId, modId } } });
    const cur = existing?.status ?? null;
    if (!FROM[op].includes(cur)) {
      const msg =
        op === "install" && (cur === "INSTALLED" || cur === "DISABLED") ? "That mod is already installed."
        : cur === null ? "That mod isn't installed."
        : `That mod is ${cur.toLowerCase()} — it can't be ${op === "remove" ? "removed" : op + "d"} right now.`;
      return { ok: false as const, error: msg };
    }
    await tx.serverMod.upsert({
      where: { serverId_modId: { serverId, modId } },
      create: { serverId, modId, status: TO_STATUS[op], error: null },
      update: { status: TO_STATUS[op], error: null },
    });
    const job = await tx.job.create({ data: { type: "GAME_MOD_SYNC", serverId, payload: { op, modId } }, select: { id: true } });
    return { ok: true as const, jobId: job.id };
  });
  if (r.ok) {
    await db.auditLog
      .create({ data: { userId: audit.userId, action: `gameserver.mod.${op}`, detail: `${serverId} mod=${audit.slug}` } })
      .catch(() => {});
  }
  return r;
}

For the restart implementation, I'm weighing whether to reuse the existing gamePower handler with a synthetic job, which is honest but creates a redundant "service restarted" notification alongside my own digest—acceptable but worth noting. I'm also considering a leaner alternative: exec-based restart using controlSpec hints instead.

Actually, reusing gamePower is better since it handles intent recording, state checks, port checks, and runtime refresh, and its forced non-retry behavior fits since my job shouldn't retry anyway—so health will be defined as gamePower success plus a serviceRunning probe, skipping log scanning for exceptions.

For version resolution, I'm sorting out priority order: Minecraft relies on McJarPin when state is ACTIVE, falling back to gameVariant/pinnedVersion or detected layout version, while Valheim treats an unset target version as "current build" with unknown resolution. I'm also noting where the version-bump hook should trigger during game updates for Minecraft.

I need to call modUpdateGameHold before the version bump to check catalog compatibility for installed AUTO-mode mods against the new game version, holding the update if any mod lacks a compatible release (ignoring unknown mod lists like Spigot). After a successful bump, I'll enqueue a mod auto-update job that runs under the per-server lock, but I'm realizing the health check fires before mods update—so incompatible mods on the new version could fail health and trigger a rollback, which is exactly why the hold exists.

I'll settle on: hold whenever the current installed mod set isn't compatible with the new version, with the message indicating whether compatible versions actually exist. Doing a fully coordinated game+mod bump would mean reimplementing versionBump's staging and rollback logic, so I'm flagging that as a follow-up rather than scope creep here.

On reflection, hard holds should only apply to mod-loader variants like Fabric, Forge, Quilt, and NeoForge — Paper plugins often list incomplete game_versions on Modrinth and generally work across versions, so blocking a Paper bump over a stale compatibility list would be too aggressive. Better to just warn for plugin variants and reserve holds for the loader mods.

For Steam-managed games like Valheim, though, I can't hold version bumps at all since they update on restart — I need an honest warning in the Updates panel explaining that we can't prevent the update, and that our post-restart rollback only reverts mods, not the game itself, so it won't help if the game update is what broke things. # Profile Upload/Download Code

**Creating/Uploading a Profile:**
```
Axios.post(
    transformPackageUrl("https://thunderstore.io/api/experimental/legacyprofile/create/"),
    payload,
    {
        headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/octet-stream' }
    }
)
```

**Downloading/Parsing a Profile:**
```
Axios.get(
    CdnProvider.addCdnQueryParameter(
        transformPackageUrl(`https://thunderstore.io/api/experimental/legacyprofile/get/${profileImportCode}/`)
    )
)
```

**Key Details:**
- Upload endpoint: `https://thunderstore.io/api/experimental/legacyprofile/create/`
- Download endpoint: `https://thunderstore.io/api/experimental/legacyprofile/get/{profileImportCode}/`
- Upload uses binary content type: `application/octet-stream`
- Response from creation includes `{ key: string }`

The provided code does not mention a specific zip filename like "export.r2x" or reference body prefixes like "#r2modman".

Based on the search results, I found information about how r2modman handles profile export and import with base64 encoding:

## Key Findings

**Profile Export Format:**
Profile exports use the .r2z (zip archive) or .r2x (raw YAML) file formats, with .r2z being a zip archive containing a YAML manifest and configuration files.

**Base64 Encoding Process:**
When converting to Base64, r2modman prepends a #r2modman header and encodes the zip as base64, then calls ProfileApiClient.createProfile() with the base64 string. The upload is the export as file encoded as base64, and downloading will convert it back to an r2z file where it's then treated like a regular file import.

**Import Process:**
Archive parsing strips the #r2modman prefix, base64-decodes, reads export.r2x (object or string versions), and collects configs from both config/ and BepInEx/config/ prefixes.

**Legacy Profile Support:**
Import accepts an .r2z file, a legacy Macheim JSON export, or a Thunderstore profile code (legacyprofile endpoint, with Hexium as fallback for Hexium-hosted codes).

The search results show that r2modman uses these components together to create a shareable payload for profile distribution.
